verdict.reasoning: Patient reports dizziness, room spinning, unsteady walking, feeling very sick (nausea), and buzzing in ears: "my room is sort of spinning and I can't walk properly... my ears are buzzing a bit. Feeling a bit off" and "I am feeling very sick."
Onset: "Started probably about two hours ago maybe" and doctor confirms "So it's there now for the past two hours, you'd say?" Patient: "Yeah."
"I had it a similar sort of thing about a month ago..." and for that episode: "Probably only about five, ten minutes."
Continuous and room-spinning: "it's there the whole time" and "my room is sort of spinning"; doctor: "like the room spinning around?" Patient: "Yeah."
"I can't walk properly. Well, I can walk properly but not straight" and "I just. I don't feel like I'm stable. The room is spinning."
"No, but I am feeling very sick" in response to being physically sick indicates nausea without vomiting; doctor labels it: "Nausea."
Doctor: "Do you have a temperature at all?" Patient: "I don't think so." This supports no reported fever.
Doctor: "Did you have any kind of viral illness in the recent past..." Patient: "No." and "No cold, cough, nothing?" Patient: "No."
Doctor: "Any kind of ear pain or ear discharge, anything like that?" Patient: "No, nothing."
"my ears are buzzing a bit" and later "It's just a bit of a buzzy noise in my ears, but otherwise I can hear everything."
Past history: "I've had premature ovarian failure and I've taken hrt."
The transcript notes premature ovarian failure and HRT in history but does not show a distinct assessment section listing this as a PMH item.
"I've had premature ovarian failure and I've taken hrt." implies the patient is/has been on hormone replacement therapy.
While HRT is mentioned, there is no explicit medication list segment labeling it as a current medication in an assessment/medication list.
Doctor: "Do you have any allergies at all?" Patient: "No."
The transcript contains no social history discussion; stating it is not documented aligns with the absence of such information.
Patient: "my legs and arms and everything are working fine" and doctor: "So there's no weakness of your arms and legs?" (implied yes). No focal weakness is described.
Patient recounts unsteadiness with spinning: "my room is sort of spinning and I can't walk properly... I don't feel like I'm stable. The room is spinning."

There is no physical ear examination performed; history only: "It's just a bit of a buzzy noise in my ears..." and "Any kind of ear pain or ear discharge...?" "No, nothing." No exam notes are recorded.
"It's just a bit of a buzzy noise in my ears, but otherwise I can hear everything" indicates hearing intact aside from tinnitus.
No objective section exists, but the patient states "I don't think so" to temperature; thus no fever is reported.
Transcript does not include any vitals; stating vital signs are not documented matches the content.
Doctor: "the most common... diagnosis... is something called labyrinthitis" and symptoms described include vertigo (room spinning), nausea ("feeling very sick"), and unsteadiness/disequilibrium.
"I had it a similar sort of thing about a month ago" describes a recurrent vertigo episode with similar presentation.
Premature ovarian failure and HRT are mentioned in history but not explicitly restated as an assessment item.
No acute infectious signs (fever, recent viral illness, ear pain/discharge) are present: patient denies viral illness, fever, and ear pain/discharge.
Doctor: "It's called semitol. Yep. It's one tablet three times a day. So I'll give you about 10 days worth..." for symptomatic relief of labyrinthitis.

Doctor: "It doesn't really matter. You can take it because sometimes... you feel a bit sick to eat anything, so might as well just take the tablets." This allows with or without food for flexible timing.
Doctor: "if you develop any weakness of your legs or arms... then, you know, you would need to take yourself to A and E." This covers new unilateral weakness as a red flag.
Doctor includes "a sudden headache" among red flag symptoms requiring A&E.
Doctor: "or you start being violently sick with it, then, you know, you would need to take yourself to A and E."
Doctor: "I would still like you to be seen by one of our doctors to take a look inside your ears to just make sure." This is a planned exam of the ears by a doctor (not necessarily ENT but a doctor).
"While you're with the doctors, we'd like to do your blood pressure..." indicates BP measurement is planned.
"While you're with the doctors, we'd like to... just examine your, you know, you know, how you're walking, and everything is." implies planned gait/neurologic assessment.

"So I'll send the prescription across to your pharmacy. It looks like it's the Lloyd Pharmacy on our system. Is that correct?" Patient: "Yeah." Doctor: "Yeah. So we'll send you across that prescription."
Doctor: "I would still like you to be seen by one of our doctors to take a look inside your ears..." is instruction to book an appointment for exam and further assessment.
Doctor: "Just make sure you call support to book that appointment. Okay?"

Doctor frames Semitol as symptomatic management: "So this is like, just symptomatic relief. Like, if you have a fever, we just give paracetamol. So just to, you know, make you able to come and see one of the doctors..."
The doctor instructs to watch for weakness, sudden headache, or violent vomiting as red flags and go to A&E, which is monitoring for red flag symptoms.
The plan is for "one of our doctors" to examine the ears; an explicit otolaryngology (ENT) specialist evaluation is not stated.

"I would still like you to be seen by one of our doctors to take a look inside your ears..." and need to "wait for the appointment for the doctor to examine you" indicate a follow-up appointment for exam and assessment.
